item.title: Repower Grisons: seasonal rates and 20 francs less for families
item.description: From 2027 in the Repower area, a typical family will spend 1,449 francs a year, -1.4% compared to 2026. Differentiated summer/winter rates and the new Optima variable option are coming soon.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Repower cuts electricity prices in its grey area - A family of 4 will pay CHF 1,449 in 2027, CHF 20 less - From 2027 differentiated energy rates per season - New Optima voluntary rate with green/yellow/red time slots
## Key facts - **What**: Slight drop in the price of electricity for domestic utilities and introduction of seasonal tariffs - When: News will start from 2027; today's communication from Repower - Where: Network area of the Repower group, mainly in Graubünden - Who: Repower, an energy group based in Poschiavo (GR) - Amount: CHF 1,449 per year for a family of 4 with consumption of 4,500 kWh (-20 CHF, -1.4%) - New: Grischunpower product with more expensive rates in winter and cheaper in summer, average annual energy price unchanged - New product: Optima, hourly variable rate with three levels (green/yellow/red) - Network investments: CHF 30-40 million per year for upgrades and smart grids
Repower, the energy group based in Poschiavo, will slightly reduce electricity prices for domestic utilities in its network area in Graubünden. The announcement came today from the company: in 2027 a family of four with an annual consumption of 4,500 kilowatt hours will pay 1,449 francs of electricity, twenty francs less than the current year. The percentage change is -1.4%.
The ## What's changing for families in Graubünden The reduction of twenty francs per year on a standard consumption of 4,500 kWh is contained — equal to 1.4% — but comes at a time when the cost of living and energy bills remain a sensitive item in the domestic budget throughout Switzerland. For a typical household, the savings amount to about 1.67 francs per month, a figure that alone does not change the structure of spending, but adds to other signs of moderation in energy prices.
It is important to underline a technical detail: the savings indicated refer to Repower's standard Grischunpower supply and do not include municipal taxes. In Graubünden — as in the rest of Switzerland — the final electricity bill consists of the sum of energy, network use, taxes and VAT. The increase in real consumption, a change of category (for example, a change to the Optima tariff) or an increase decided by the individual municipalities can easily cancel or exceed the twenty francs of savings indicated.
### Seasonal Differentiation: Opportunity and Attention The logic of the differentiated tariff is well known: shifting consumption in the summer months, when hydroelectric and solar production is more abundant, is in the best interest of both the customer and the grid. Repower explains this by recalling the greater availability of renewable energy in the summer and the trend of the electricity markets.
For a Grisonese family, the practical question becomes: when is it best to move loads?
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## What to do now if you are a Repower customer in Graubünden The changes will take effect on 1 January 2027, but customers can start preparing in advance by checking three concrete aspects of their supply.
### Check your consumption profile First step: download or request from Repower the details of your monthly consumption over the last two years. With the new seasonal tariff structure, knowing how much energy you consume between December and February compared to June-August becomes crucial to estimating the impact on your 2027 bill. If your consumption is concentrated in winter, get ready for more marked seasonal peaks; if it is spread out, the effect will be neutral on the annual total.
### Decide whether Optima is right for you Second step: assess whether the variable Optima tariff suits your lifestyle. It is especially worthwhile for those who have a smart meter, an electric vehicle, or a heat pump and can shift loads to green hours. It is not suitable for those who have no scheduling flexibility: in that case, the risk is paying for red hours without being able to avoid them. Repower will make the quarterly time bands available in advance, so planning is possible but requires attention.
### Check the municipal levies Third step: remember that the bill also includes municipal levies, which Repower charges on behalf of the municipalities. A possible increase in the municipal multiplier can wipe out the announced twenty-franc saving. Check your municipality's website for the 2027 tariffs as soon as they are published.
### When the official communication will arrive Repower announced the changes with a statement today; personalised letters with the new prices and any switch to Optima should be sent out in the coming months, as per standard practice in the sector. If you do not receive any communication by autumn 2026, contact the group's customer service directly.

item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in Canton Uri
item.description: How to find an internship in Canton Uri: contract, salary, professional maturity and concrete steps to apply.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - In Switzerland, vocational training is regulated at the federal level by the LFPr - The Canton of Uri manages the network of traineeship posts through the cantonal office of vocational training - Apprenticeship normally takes place in 3 or 4 years, depending on the profession - Federal professional maturity is compatible with the internship and opens the doors to sup
## Key facts - **What**: dual vocational training (company + vocational school + intercompany courses) - When: 3- or 4-year internship, with the possibility of parallel professional maturity - Where: Canton Uri, cantonal vocational training authority - Who: UST/BFS for federal statistics, State Secretariat for Training (SEFRI) for legal bases - Amount: the apprentice's salary is set by the employer according to the sector and the year of internship (cantonal reference rates, annual amount to be verified year by year)
Vocational training in Switzerland is based on a federal legal basis, the Vocational Training Act (LFPr), and is divided into three places of learning: the training company, the vocational school and intercompany courses. In the Uri Canton, as in the rest of the Confederation, this dual model allows those who finish compulsory school to choose a qualified professional path directly, without necessarily going through high school. The watchword is permeability: after a federal certificate ## # Finding an internship: concrete channels The search for an internship position in Canton Uri passes through some standard channels. The first is the Cantonal Vocational Training Office, which publishes the list of available traineeships every year and accompanies young people in their choice. The second is the national platform Orientamento.ch, which gathers offers from all Swiss training companies. The third is direct contact with companies, often the most effective in smaller cantons such as URIs, where the economic fabric is made up of many SMEs.
A good practice is to start the research one year before the start of the internship. Training companies select candidates in the spring for the beginning of the following summer, although deadlines vary from industry to industry. For the craft and technical sectors — particularly present in a mountain canton such as Uri — spontaneous applications are often well received, especially if accompanied by an updated curriculum vitae and a personalised letter of motivation.
### Internship contract: what it must contain The traineeship contract is governed by the Code of Obligations (CO) and the Vocational Training Ordinance (OFPr). It must indicate the duration, the monthly or annual salary of the apprentice, the weekly working hours, the days of vacation (minimum 4 weeks, 5 weeks for those under 20), the person responsible for training in
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete application procedure: step by step For those who want to start an apprenticeship in Canton Uri, the realistic path unfolds in six steps.
1. Self-assessment and choice of profession. Consult the official list of available professions at the Cantonal Office of Vocational Education and the guidance tools at orientamento.ch. It is also useful to do a trial internship at a company to test the chosen profession.
2. Active search for an apprenticeship position. Send written applications to companies in the sector, register on the cantonal platform for apprenticeship positions, and contact directly the guidance office of the secondary school.
**3. Presentation interview.** Present yourself with a portfolio of school assessments, internship certificates, and personal references. Small Uri-based companies often also assess personal motivation and knowledge of the local area.
4. Signing of the apprenticeship contract. Check that the contract specifies: profession, duration, salary, weekly working hours, holidays, vocational school, and the contact person at the company. Keep a copy signed by both parties.
5. Registration at the vocational school. The company normally forwards the data to the school, but the apprentice (or whoever holds parental authority, if a minor) must confirm the registration.
6. Registration with social insurance. The company registers the apprentice with the mandatory insurances: AVS/AHV, accident insurance (LAINF/LAA), AD/AC, and pension fund if the coordinated salary exceeds the LPP/BVG threshold. In Canton Uri as in the rest of Switzerland, anyone who changes canton or begins a gainful activity must also take out mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) within three months.
### Mistakes to avoid Underestimating the time needed for the search is the most frequent mistake: many companies close selections in spring. Not carefully reading the federal ordinance for the chosen profession leads to discovering exam subjects or admission conditions too late. Finally, not considering the vocational baccalaureate at the time of signing the contract can later force more complicated schooling choices.
For those who are already employed and want to compare their payslip with average sector rates, it is useful to use the calculation tools available on our site. To calculate the net salary of an apprentice — taking into account AVS/AHV, AD/AC, LAINF/LAA and LPP/BVG deductions — start from the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) and enter the gross annual salary agreed in the apprenticeship contract.

item.title: Energy transition, Switzerland is fifth in Europe but wind remains weak
item.description: Study SES 2025: 4872 kWh per capita from renewables, solar at 878 kWh. Wind stopped at 18 kWh, 25th place out of 28 countries.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Switzerland fifth in the EU for renewables per capita: 4872 kWh - Solar: new record at 878 kWh per capita, tenth place - Wind: only 18 kWh per capita, 25th place out of 28 countries - 70.8% of the electricity consumed in Switzerland is renewable
## Key facts - **What**: annual ranking of renewable energy production per capita - When: 2025 data, published today (study dated yesterday) - Where: comparison between Switzerland and 27 EU Member States - Who: Schweizerische Energie-Stiftung (SES), Swiss Energy Foundation - Study title: Dekarbonisierung der schweizer Energieversorgung im Europäischen Vergleich - Per capita solar amount CH: 878 kWh (historical record) - Wind energy per capita CH: 18 kWh - Renewable share of electricity consumption CH: 70.8%
The Swiss energy transition runs, but at two speeds. The Schweizerische Energie-Stiftung (SES) puts it in black and white in the annual study "Dekarbonisierung der schweizer Energieversorgung im Europäischen Vergleich", which for 2025 compares the Confederation with the 27 countries of the European Union. The verdict is positive overall, with the fifth place for electricity production from renewable sources per capita: 4,872 kilowatt-hours (kWh), behind Sweden (11,478 kWh), Finland (8,245), Austria (6,655) and Denmark (5,066).
The Swiss figure, SES explains, is mainly based on hydroelectric power, which alone generates more than half of the current produced in Switzerland. If you report the ## Analysis: what it means for bills and the Swiss energy mix
The picture that emerges from the SES study is a half-full glass, with an obvious crack on the wind side. The Confederation can boast a continental record in the share of renewables in electricity consumption: 70.8%, of which almost 55 percentage points come from hydropower and around 13 from solar power. A figure that earns it fifth place in Europe, behind Sweden (92%), Austria (88%), Denmark (82%) and Portugal (71%). In practical terms, seven kWh out of every ten consumed in Switzerland come from sun, water or wind.
### Electrification still low
There is, however, another indicator that tempers the enthusiasm: the overall degree of electrification of the energy system. Electricity accounts for 26.7% of total energy consumption in Switzerland, seventh in the SES ranking. The record goes to Sweden, which still stops at 35.3%: a sign that most of the energy consumed in Europe still depends on other sources, not necessarily green. For the Confederation, therefore, the challenge is twofold: producing more clean electricity and, at the same time, shifting to electricity those segments currently dominated by fossil fuels, such as heating and transport.
### Where Switzerland can still grow
The study stresses that the Confederation has a not insignificant expansion potential. Per capita figures in several more northerly countries, where solar irradiation is objectively lower, remain higher. In other words: with fewer hours of sunlight, more solar kWh are produced, showing that the technical growth margin — between permits, available roofs and ground-mounted systems — is there.
On the wind front, however, the recent acceleration of authorisation procedures and several projects in the pipeline could allow a partial recovery of the accumulated delay, notes SES. The reference is to federal simplifications aimed at unblocking processes that have been stalled for years, a hot political topic in Parliament and in the Alpine cantons.
### SES's requests to policymakers
"It is essential that politics guarantees framework conditions (for all green vectors) in the long term. Only in this way will it be possible to stimulate the necessary investments and durably carry forward the progress of the energy transition," SES writes in the press release accompanying the study. A request that closely concerns companies and investors called upon to plan plants with twenty-year horizons, and that weighs directly on the cost of energy for households and SMEs in the coming years.
For those who want to understand how much bills weigh on the family budget today, it is useful to compare the data on the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) and simulate the effect of electricity tariffs on the payslip with the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## What to do: the role of households, Cantons and investors
The 2025 SES study does not provide individual recipes, but it draws a clear perimeter within which households, Cantons and operators move. Here are the operational points that emerge from the data.
### For households
Taking advantage of the record photovoltaic figures is worthwhile, especially in a country where over 96% of new installations are rooftop-based. The balance between self-consumption and grid feed-in remains the key factor in reducing energy expenditure, an issue that directly affects the household [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living). In recent years the Confederation has introduced mechanisms for reimbursing the repurchase tariff, and several Cantons offer stackable cantonal incentives. Before installing a system, it is worth checking both the municipal regulations and the cantonal rates, because the difference in tax treatment between the energy component and excise duties varies from Canton to Canton.
### For Cantons and municipalities
The wind power figure (18 kWh per capita) and the recent acceleration of authorisation procedures indicate where the next few years will be decided. Alpine and pre-Alpine municipalities, in particular, remain the decisive hubs: without their technical and political green light, projects stay stuck. For local authorities, the challenge is intertwined with spatial planning, ecological compensation, and the share of taxes and water royalties linked to renewable production.
### For businesses and investors
Demand for solar and wind installations is clearly accelerating. According to SES, Swiss solar production increased by 2000 GWh in a single year, and the foundation's request is for stable, long-term framework conditions. For those considering an investment in the sector, three checks are essential: technical feasibility of the site, the cantonal and municipal authorisation process, and the subsidy or grid feed-in reimbursement regime.
### Scenario: what would change with more wind power
Taking wind seriously would mean closing the gap with Austria, Luxembourg and Hungary, which today produce far more electricity from wind. If Switzerland reached at least the Austrian per capita level, the share of renewables in electricity consumption would rise well beyond the current 70.8%, moving closer to Sweden (92%) and Austria (88%). The benefit would translate into lower dependence on imports during the winter months, with direct effects on the wholesale electricity price and, in turn, on the tariffs paid by households and businesses.
To simulate the impact of a different expense structure on your net salary, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator): enter your gross annual income and compare scenarios with and without deductions for energy expenses and commuting. For those who want to keep up with labour market news linked to the green transition, the [job listings](nav:jobs) section collects open positions in the energy sector and related supply chains.

item.description: Two initiatives on the ballot on 27 September: neutrality and nutrition. The Federal Financial Controller records a budget of CHF 7.88 million.

The federal voting round on September 27 mobilizes considerable financial resources. The committees involved in the two items on the ballot declared total budgets of almost 8 million francs, according to data published by the Federal Financial Control (EFK). For those living and working in Switzerland, the rules on campaign financing transparency offer the possibility to inform yourself before voting. The Swiss Federal Audit Office (EFK) publishes data on financing declarations, accessible to anyone who wants to verify who economically supports the various positions at stake.
### How the declaration works
Committees that spend more than 50,000 francs on a voting campaign must submit a declaration to the Swiss Federal Audit Office. In this declaration, all contributions received must be indicated, with separate evidence of donors who contribute sums equal to or greater than 15,000 francs. The data is then made public by the EFK, typically in the weeks preceding the vote.
This system allows voters to evaluate not only the arguments of campaigns, but also the economic and political interests that lie behind each position. A side that raises funds primarily from the food industry, for example, may have economic reasons to oppose an initiative that could affect prices or industry regulations.
### What to do concretely
Before each federal vote, you can consult the EFK website to verify declared funding. The procedure is simple: access the EFK portal, search for the September 27 vote, and download the declaration documents for each committee. item.title: CDF: 7.86 million for voting campaigns 27 September
item.description: The Federal Financial Controller publishes the budgets: 5.51 million for neutrality, 2.35 million for food. Blocker 2+ mln, Economiesuisse 1.2 mln.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - CDF: CHF 7.86 million total campaign budget vote 27 September - Neutrality initiative: 5.51 million (3.84 yes, 1.67 no) - Food initiative: 2.35 million (0.72 yes, 1.63 no) - Blocker 2+ mln, Economiesuisse 1.2 mln against neutrality
## Key facts - **What**: Federal Voting Campaign Budget Statement - When: Votes 27 September, data communicated today - Where: Switzerland, federal level - Who: Federal Financial Control (FFC) - Amount: 7.86 million francs in total
The Federal Financial Control (FFC) has announced the budgets declared by the referendum committees in view of the federal votes on September 27. The total figure stands at CHF 7.86 million, with a clear prevalence of resources concentrated on the Neutrality Initiative, which alone absorbs CHF 5.51 million. The Food Initiative collects the remaining 2.35 million. The data, as specified by the CDF, are not definitive: the authority has yet to carry out additional checks and recalls that sometimes the same payment can be declared twice, first as own funds and then as a donation to another organisation.
### Marked asymmetry on the Neutrality Initiative The "yes" side of the initiative "Safeguarding Swiss Neutrality" has 3.84 million, financed by the "Preservation of Swiss Neutrality" committee. Two donors weigh in decisively: former UDC Federal Councillor Christoph Blocher paid out of pocket The disparity of resources between the two fronts on each initiative offers a concrete glimpse into the balances of economic power behind the Swiss referendum campaigns. On neutrality, the ratio is about 2.3 to 1 in favor of "yes", driven by two well-known private actors; on food, the ratio is about 2.3 to 1 for "no", with the weight of agricultural and agro-industrial organizations. This asymmetry is not a new phenomenon, but the CDF numbers make it measurable and transparent to the electorate.
### Transparency and limits of the current system The reporting mechanism managed by the CDF represents the main instrument of financial accountability in the Swiss direct democracy. However, the CDF itself points out two structural limits: the figures are not definitive at the time of publication and the double counting of certain payments can artificially inflate the totals. For the citizen, this means that the data should be read as a provisional photograph, not as a certified balance sheet. The Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) does not intervene in this survey, which remains the exclusive competence of the CDF.

## Key facts - **What**: Prosecution for bribery of foreign public officials and aggravated money laundering - Who: Pierre Mirabaud, former president of the Swiss Bankers Association (SBA) 2003-2009 - When: Hearing begins in September; disputed facts between 2000 and 2012; investigation initiated in 2021 - Where: Federal Criminal Court (TPF) in Bellinzona; investigation by the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPC) - Counterpart: President of the Public Institution for Social Security (PIFSS) of Kuwait, an entity comparable to the Swiss AVS - Amount disputed: 82 million francs of promised retrocessions - Funds managed: about 500 million dollars (about 400 million francs) entrusted to the Mirabaud bank - Compensation: 42 million francs already paid to PIFSS - Penalty requested: 24 months suspended with probation
Pierre Mirabaud, former president of the Swiss Bankers' Association (ASB) between 2003 and 2009, will be tried in early September by the Federal Criminal Court (TPF) on charges of bribery of foreign public officials and aggravated money laundering. This is reported by the Keystone-ATS agency, which obtained a copy of the indictment.
### ## A story that touches the Swiss financial centre The case comes at a time of increasing attention to the conduct of Swiss institutions in foreign markets, particularly in the area of asset management on behalf of sovereign wealth funds and public social security institutions. The news directly concerns the reputation of a private Geneva bank with historical roots in the Swiss financial landscape.
## # Dispute Numbers The indictment sets two precise economic thresholds. On the one hand, the alleged undue retrocessions, quantified at 82 million francs, corresponding to about 20% of the funds entrusted by the Kuwaiti entity. On the other hand, the compensation already made, amounting to 42 million francs. It remains unspecified in the source whether this sum is the result of a pact with the power of attorney or a unilateral defense initiative, nor any additional amounts disputed by way of compensation.
### What is disputed on a legal level The cases of crime — bribery of foreign public officials and aggravated money laundering — are among the typical cases prosecuted by the MPC against Swiss financial operators active abroad. The penalty requested, 24 months suspended with the conditional sentence, reflects the choice of the simplified procedure and the recognition of the facts by the defendant. The source does not specify whether the judgment also includes typical ancillary measures in the area of corruption and money laundering, such as disqualification

The following remain unspecified in the source: the exact date of the start of the hearing, the possible quantification of the confiscation, the timing of the filing of the sentence and the possible appeal.

item.title: SNB, here's what the new francs will look like from 2030
item.description: The SNB chose the graphic design "J" by Emphase for the tenth series of banknotes: six denominations, with an altitude theme, in circulation in the early 2030s.

## In a nutshell - BNS has chosen the graphic design for the tenth series of banknotes - Expected entry into circulation in the early 2030s - Theme: "Switzerland, variety in relief", a journey through altitudes - Winner: Emphase Sagl, team Kilchör and Fasel
## Key facts - **What**: Selection of the graphic design for the tenth series of Swiss banknotes - When: BNS announcement, entered into circulation in the early 2030s - Where: Switzerland, designed by the SNB in Bern and Zurich - Who: Swiss National Bank (SNB); winner Emphase Sagl - Project: drawn up by J, led by Fabienne Kilchör and Sébastien Fasel - Theme: "Switzerland, variety in relief" - Final decision: Bank Council of the SNB - Safety: to be developed in the coming years
The Swiss National Bank has chosen the graphic design destined to become the tenth series of Swiss banknotes. The winner of the competition held by the SNB was Drafted J, developed by the Emphase Sagl studio under the guidance of Fabienne Kilchör and Sébastien Fasel. The new banknotes, with a total of six denominations, will enter into circulation "as soon as possible at the beginning of the 2030s", as specified by the issuing institution.
The images presented in these days are not yet the final ones: the Bank Council of the SNB will have to express itself on the final role after a phase of graphic, content and above all security development, which will require "the next few years". Current tickets, fruit ### Why the altitude theme speaks to all of Switzerland
The choice to tell Switzerland's story through altitude bands is not a stylistic exercise: it means crossing in six cuts the 4,850 metres that separate Lake Maggiore's water level from the 4,810 metres of the Dufourspitze, touching at least four of the six biogeographical regions recognised at federal level. It is an idea that enhances Swiss polycentrism, where the Confederation coexists with 26 cantons and roughly 2,100 municipalities, each with its own landscape identity. For an economy built on tourism, mountain agriculture, cutting-edge research and logistics infrastructure — from Alpine passes to freight rail corridors such as the Gotthardo — the narrative by altitudes translates into images what the macroeconomic figures from the FSO have been showing for years: the country's wealth is distributed across the entire vertical gradient, not only along the Zurich–Geneva–Basel axes.
### Practical implications for those who use the franc every day
For those who live and work in Switzerland the change will not hit wallets immediately: the ninth series will remain legal tender and no current banknote will be withdrawn in the coming years. What will change, gradually, is the user experience: cashiers, merchants and consumers will need to familiarise themselves with new graphic elements and, above all, with previously unseen security features — the most delicate chapter of any SNB issue, designed to resist counterfeiting.
An often overlooked aspect concerns machines: vending machines, parking meters, SBB ticket machines, turnstiles and ticket validators will need to be adapted to recognise the new banknotes. In previous series the SNB coordinated the transition with key sectors — banks, the postal service, public transport, large-scale retail — to minimise disruption. It is reasonable to expect a similar timetable for the tenth series as well, with pilot tests and gradual adjustments in the months before the launch.
### Scenario: what happens from 2030 onwards
When the tenth series enters circulation in the early 2030s, old banknotes will remain exchangeable for an extended period — the established practice in all previous SNB issues. The issuing institution, headquartered in Bern and Zurich, will manage the dual circulation until the last specimen of the ninth series has been returned to the central bank's coffers. For businesses that handle large volumes of cash — retail, restaurants, transport — the operational advice remains the same as in previous transitions: avoid investing heavily in single-series devices before the official rollout schedule, which the SNB will communicate with ample advance notice. For those who want to start gauging the impact on their household budget, it can be useful to begin with the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to understand how the cost of living varies across the country's different altitudes, from Mittelland cities to Alpine villages.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What to do now: a three-step guide
The SNB announcement does not impose any mandatory action today, but it is the right time to prepare for a change that will become part of the daily life of all Swiss residents and anyone working on Swiss soil.
1. Keep using the current banknotes. The ninth series, introduced in 2016, remains legal tender. No banknote currently in circulation loses value or validity with the announcement of the tenth series' design project. Any concerns about obsolescence are therefore premature.
2. Follow the upcoming institutional steps. The SNB's Bank Council — the institution's decision-making body — will have to approve the final design of the new banknotes. The current phase is still focused on graphic and content development, and above all on security. The specifications for the six denominations from 10 to 1,000 francs, including the details of the subjects on each denomination, have not yet been released and will be communicated by the SNB over the coming years.
3. Prepare on the operational side, both in business and at home. When the SNB publishes the issuance schedule — typically with at least 12 to 18 months' notice — vending machines, ATMs, ticket machines, and validators will need to be updated. For small businesses and retailers, it is advisable to wait for the official SNB guidelines before purchasing new devices or replacing existing equipment, as already happened during the transitions between the seventh, eighth, and ninth series.

For those who want to understand the concrete impact of the franc on their budget — including salaries, taxes, health insurance premiums, and the cost of living at Switzerland's different altitudes — the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) makes it possible to simulate net pay and the effect of social and tax deductions. ## FAQ
When will the new Swiss banknotes enter circulation? The Swiss National Bank has announced that the tenth series of banknotes will be put into circulation 'at the earliest at the beginning of the 2030s'. This is an indicative horizon: the SNB's Bank Council will still have to approve the final design after a phase of graphic and security development that will take several years. The ninth series, introduced in 2016, will remain legal tender until its complete withdrawal.
Who won the design competition for the tenth series? The winner was design J, developed by the studio Emphase Sagl under the guidance of Fabienne Kilchör and Sébastien Fasel. The project is titled 'Switzerland, variety in relief' and tells the story of the country through its different altitudinal levels. On the front of each denomination, an indigenous plant will appear, while the back will feature infrastructure, architecture, and symbols of Swiss life.
What changes for cash users in Switzerland? In the short term, nothing: current banknotes remain valid. When the tenth series enters circulation, vending machines, cash registers, ticket machines, and validators will need to be adapted to the new denominations and new security features, as already happened during the transitions between previous series. For individuals and businesses, the advice is to follow the SNB guidelines that will be published well in advance of the launch.

## In a nutshell - Family allowances in Switzerland are governed by the LAFam (Federal Act on Family Allowances) - Each canton, including Uri, fixes the amounts of checks and manages its own compensation fund - The Confederation only establishes minimum amounts valid throughout the national territory - The amounts and the application procedure in the Canton of Uri follow the relevant cantonal law
## Key facts - **What**: Framework of family and training allowances in the Canton of Uri, with amounts, legal conditions and application procedure - When: Current regulatory framework (exact date of last modification not specified in the source) - Where: Canton of Uri, Switzerland; federal law applicable throughout the Confederation - Who: Confederation (federal law), Canton of Uri (cantonal law and recognized family compensation funds), employers and beneficiaries (salaried, self-employed, non-lucrative persons) - Amount: Federal minimum amounts LAFam and cantonal amounts uri — not specified in the source with exact figures - Legal basis: LAFam (Federal Law on Family Allowances) at federal level, Cantonal Law on Family Allowances of the Canton of Uri - Federal Tax Office: Federal Office of Social Insurance (UFAS) — responsible for social security, NOT for taxation
The Canton of Uri regulates family and training allowances on the basis of the Federal Law on Family Allowances ## Because Uri is an interesting case on the national scene
The Swiss system of family allowances is characterized by a mixed structure: a common federal base (LAFam) and strong cantonal variability in amounts and coffers. This architecture means that two families residing in neighbouring cantons can receive different amounts on equal terms. Uri, a small Alpine canton, falls within this logic and applies its own cantonal legislation, with family compensation funds recognised by the canton.
### Difference between federal minimum amounts and cantonal amounts
LAFam sets national minimum amounts for the child allowance and the training allowance. These amounts represent the floor under which no canton can go down, but most cantons — including Uri — pay higher amounts. The source does not specify either the updated federal minimum amounts or those practiced in the Canton of Uri, so the article merely describes the mechanism, referring the reader to official sources for exact values.
### Who is entitled and from when
The right to family allowances arises from the month in which the child is born or received into the family, and normally ends at the age of 16 for the child allowance, and at the age of 25 for the training allowance (if the child is still in training). Source does not indicate Canton of Uri specific exceptions to this rule
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## Concrete procedure for requesting family allowances in the Canton of Uri
The application procedure for family allowances in Switzerland follows similar logic in all cantons, with cantonal adaptations regarding forms and the competent compensation fund. Uri is no exception: the applicant must contact the recognized family compensation fund and submit the application with the required documents.
### Step 1: identify the competent compensation fund
The first concrete step is to understand which fund to contact. For an employee, the fund is normally the employer's fund. A self-employed worker must register with the professional or cantonal family compensation fund designated by the Canton of Uri. A person without gainful activity who is entitled to allowances must contact the cantonal fund. The source does not indicate the name and address of the Uri cantonal fund, but the information can be obtained from the Uri cantonal administration.
### Step 2: gather the necessary documents
The application typically requires: identity document, certificate of family status or family register extract, children's birth certificates, education certificate for children over 16, and — for self-employed workers — documentation of income from gainful activity. For foreign citizens, a residence or permanent residence permit issued by the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) is also required.
### Step 3: submit the application
The application is submitted to the competent family compensation fund. In many cases, the employer automatically starts paying the allowances, but it is good practice to verify that registration has been completed. Funds may request additional documents in case of special situations (custody, spouse's children, separation, work activity in several cantons).
### Step 4: verify the amount actually paid
Once the allowance has been obtained, it is advisable to check the amount actually credited on the pay slip and compare it with what is provided for by Uri cantonal law. Any differences can be reported to the compensation fund. In case of disagreement on contributions, the BSV (Federal Social Insurance Office) is the federal body responsible for social insurance — NOT the FTA, which deals with federal taxation.
### When the entitlement ends
The right to family allowances ends when the child turns 16 (child allowance) or 25 (education allowance, if education ends earlier). In case of termination of gainful activity or transfer to another canton, the fund must be informed promptly.

item.title: National exhibitions: yes to the message, no co-financing until 2040
item.description: The Federal Council approves on 26 August 2026 the message on the new law: maximum federal contribution at 30% and parliamentary decision no earlier than 2035.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Law on National Exhibitions: message approved on 26 August 2026 - No federal co-financing before 2040, confirmed by the Federal Council - Maximum federal contribution: 30% of eligible costs - Parliament may decide whether and when to co-finance, but not before 2035
## Key facts - **What**: Approval of the message on the new federal law on national exhibitions - When: 26 August 2026 - Where: Bern - Who: Federal Council - Mandate: CSEC-S Motion 23.3966, approved by Parliament in March 2024 - Time limit: Federal co-financing excluded before 2040 - Maximum federal share: 30% of eligible costs - Opinions collected in consultation: 52
### The decision of August 26, 2026 The Federal Council approved on 26 August 2026 the message regarding the new Federal Law on the Promotion of National Exhibitions. The text of the law lays the foundations for possible financial support by the Confederation for future national exhibitions, thus fulfilling the mandate of a motion approved by Parliament.
At the same time, the Executive confirmed its decision, taken in June 2025, not to co-finance such an exposure before 2040. The choice reflects the current spending priorities of the Confederation: in the coming years there are no resources to commit to a major event of this magnitude, even if the legal framework conditions are still defined.
### The role of ### What concretely changes for Cantons and Municipalities The new law redraws the perimeter of who can apply for federal funds for a national exposure and under what conditions. Before this message, the rules were not codified in a single text: each initiative was based on political decisions on a case-by-case basis. With the new federal law on the promotion of national exhibitions, the picture becomes explicit: no federal money without a concrete project, without a cantonal and municipal quota at least equivalent, and without a decision in principle of Parliament.
For a Canton wishing to apply to host a national exhibition, the message clarifies three operational aspects. First, the project must be sufficiently mature before applying for federal co-financing. Second: Cantons and Municipalities must guarantee at least 30% of the eligible costs, equal to the maximum federal share, so in fact the required co-financing ratio is one to one. Third: the Confederation does not issue deficit guarantees, exposing the promoters to the risk of covering any budget holes.
### The calendar that comes out of the message The roadmap set by the message is clear. The decision of parliamentary principle cannot be proposed before 2035. Federal co-financing, therefore, cannot materialize before 2040. For those who today think about the next national exhibition, it means taking into account a horizon
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What happens now: the institutional roadmap After the approval of the dispatch of 26 August 2026, the text goes to the Federal Assembly. The relevant parliamentary committees will examine it, and then the plenary of each Chamber will vote on it. Only after the law's possible entry into force will the Federal Council be able to propose, not before 2035, a principle decision to Parliament on a single national exposition project.
For the promoting bodies, the operational path is structured as follows:
1. Define a concrete project with costs, timelines, and territorial impact. 2. Ensure the formal involvement of the host Cantons and Municipalities, with a co-financing share at least equivalent to the federal contribution requested. 3. Submit the application when the project is sufficiently mature, at a time when the political and economic framework makes a principle decision by Parliament plausible. 4. Plan in the financial framework for the absence of a deficit guarantee from the Confederation: any shortfalls remain the responsibility of the promoting bodies, the Cantons, and the Municipalities.
### What to watch in the coming months The first concrete milestone is the start of the parliamentary process. The Science, Education and Culture Committees (CSEC) and the Finance Committees will be called upon to examine the dispatch. The umbrella associations of the Municipalities and Cantons, which took part in the consultation, will follow the dossier to see whether the criticisms of the funding model will lead to amendments.
Another aspect to monitor is Parliament's position on the 2035 date as the threshold for the principle decision. The constraint is currently in the Federal Council's dispatch: it is up to the Chambers to modify it, but the Executive has made clear that its intention is to hold firm on 2040 as the minimum horizon.

Obtaining a type C residence permit in Canton Uri is a key step for foreigners wishing to settle permanently in Switzerland. This permit, unlike the B residence permit, confers broader rights and greater stability, bringing the holder closer to full integration into the Swiss social and economic fabric. In order to apply for the C permit in Canton Uri, a continuous residence in Switzerland for a period of ten years is generally required, of which at least five consecutive in the canton itself. For citizens of European Union (EU) and European Free Trade Association (EFTA) countries, time requirements can be reduced, often to five years of total residence in Switzerland, with some of these spent in the canton. This concept of integration is multifaceted and includes several practical aspects that the cantonal authorities assess. First of all, economic stability is a fundamental pillar: the applicant must be able to support himself and his family without resorting to social aid. This implies a stable employment or a sufficient and lasting source of income. The procedure for obtaining a C residence permit in the Canton of Uri follows a well-defined process, primarily managed by the Cantonal Office for Immigration and Labour (Ausländer- und Integrationsamt). There is also the possibility of requesting an early issuance of the C residence permit, even before the ten years of residence are completed. Generally, early issuance is granted if the applicant demonstrates a strong connection to Switzerland, for example, through marriage to Swiss citizens, children born in Switzerland attending school, or exceptional professional and social integration. The final decision rests with the cantonal authorities, who act in accordance with federal directives. ## In a nutshell - Permit B issued by Canton Uri, normally for 5 years and renewable - National regulatory reference: Federal Law on Foreigners (LStr) - Cantonal competence: Migration Office of Canton Uri - Typical documents: passport, employment contract, accommodation certificate
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit B (Aufenthaltsbewilligung B / permis de séjour B) for foreign nationals in Canton Uri - When: Initial duration up to 5 years, then periodic renewals; renewal terms not yet specified - Where: Canton Uri (Altdorf), cantonal migration office - Who: SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) at federal level; cantonal migration services for implementation - Amount: Cantonal issuance/renewal fees not specified in the source
Residence permit B is governed by the Federal Law on Foreigners (LStr) and is issued in Switzerland by each Canton. In the Uri Canton, operational responsibility lies with the Cantonal Migration Office, which works in agreement with the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) in Bern. The B permit is intended for foreign nationals residing in Switzerland with a long-term residence intention, usually linked to a work activity or family reunification, and is granted for an initial duration that can reach up to five years, with subsequent possibility of renewal.
### Who releases and what is needed In Canton Uri, the procedure begins with the ### What changes for residents in Canton Uri Obtaining and maintaining a B permit involves a series of recurring obligations that affect everyday life. The holder is required to notify the Migration Office of any relevant change: change of employer, change of domicile, changes in marital status, birth of children. Failure to update this information may jeopardise renewal. For non-EU/EFTA citizens, the issuance of the B permit is often tied to a specific employment relationship: job loss must be reported promptly and may affect the residence title.
### Cost of living and cantonal integration Living in Canton Uri means dealing with a more contained housing market than in the major Swiss urban centres, but it is still governed by federal law on tenancy (art. 253 ff. CO). The deposit may amount to up to three months' rent and must be paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name. On the healthcare front, mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) must be taken out within three months of arrival, with a per-capita premium that varies by canton and region; for adults, deductibles ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 are available, and the Canton grants premium reductions based on income.
### Practical scenario: from first issuance to first renewal A worker who obtains a B permit in Canton Uri for the first time generally receives it for an initial duration of up to five years, unless revoked for reasons provided by law. Before expiry, the Migration Office usually sends a communication with renewal instructions. The applicant must submit updated documentation (extract from the civil status register, certificate of residence, proof of employment) and, in some cases, demonstrate linguistic and social integration. If the requirements remain unchanged, the permit is renewed under the same conditions; otherwise, the authority may limit the duration or revoke the title.
To check the consequences of renewal on your payslip and social contributions (AVS/AHV, LPP/BVG, AD/AC, LAINF/UVG), it is worth using the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).

The actual steps and exact documents must always be confirmed with the Migration Office of Canton Uri.
1. Collection of documents: valid passport, biometrics, employment contract or binding offer, proof of accommodation, civil status certificates if necessary. 2. Submission of the application to the Migration Office of Canton Uri (Altdorf), with the cantonal form duly completed. 3. Verification of the requirements by the cantonal service, in agreement with the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) regarding quotas and allocations. 4. The Federal Office of Culture (UFC) has confirmed the renewal of support for film festivals of national importance in Switzerland. The decision covers the period 2027–2029 and guarantees financial continuity for ten festivals including the famous Locarno Film Festival, which will receive 1.73 million francs per year. Federal structural contributions are not one-off handouts, but multi-year investments that allow festivals to plan their activities with a time horizon of at least three years. In broader terms, structural funding serves three purposes: first, to stabilize the national cultural offering; second, to strengthen Swiss cinematic identity in international markets; third, to generate local economic spillover (employment, tourism, and income for hotels and restaurants). In the case of Locarno, the Ticino city benefits from a flow of visitors linked to the festival that translates into measurable economic returns.

As Locarno itself states, the festival «offers a privileged showcase for Swiss cinema, fostering its circulation in international markets for the benefit of the country's audiovisual production». This statement encapsulates the strategic objectives of federal funding: it is not simply support for an event, but a lever for promoting the Swiss audiovisual industry in a global context.
Swiss filmmaking competes on a worldwide level and needs visible platforms. Locarno, with its history and reputation, offers exactly that. ### Motion Chronicle
The Federal Council approves the motion by Ticino National Councillor Alex Farinelli that aims to regulate rate increases for streaming platforms such as Netflix. The federal executive recommends that Parliament support this initiative to protect Swiss consumers from unilateral price increases.
In recent years, subscription digital service providers have made repeated price increases using very permissive terms and conditions that give them ample leeway to act unilaterally. This approach contradicts the fundamental principle that a market economy works only if the contractual rules are predictable, understandable and applied in good faith.

The motion represents a significant change in the relationship between streaming service providers and users. With the approval of the motion, the situation would change radically. Suppliers would be obliged to specify in the contract itself the exact criteria on which any future price increases will be based. A generic clause is no longer enough: the criteria must be objective and transparent, established before the customer subscribes.

Italy and Germany have already shown that this regulation is possible. Both countries have taken specific measures to limit arbitrary increases in the prices of streaming platforms. Their experience shows that well-constructed regulation protects consumers without paralyzing the market.

## In a nutshell - Center for unmanned systems with tech hub and military command from 2026 - Drone battalion operational since 2028 with its own recruit school - Investments in drone defense to protect critical infrastructure
## Key facts - **What**: Center for unmanned systems (tech hub + military command) - When: 27 August 2026 (announcement); operational battalion from 2028 - Where: Switzerland at federal level, in collaboration with cantons and private individuals - Who: DDPS (Federal Department of Defence, Population Protection and Sport) - References: Defence guidelines 19 June 2026; army message 2026; armament programme 2027
On 27 August 2026, the Federal Department of Defence, Population Protection and Sport (DDPS) announced a strategic breakthrough: drones, drone defence and robotics become national priorities to strengthen Switzerland's military capabilities.
The decision responds to a changed threat situation. Drones, powered by artificial intelligence, have radically transformed the way wars are conducted. In Switzerland, there is an increase in drone flights over military and critical infrastructure. At the same time, drones assert themselves as a tool of hybrid warfare, a mode of conflict that goes beyond the traditional military confrontation.
### Three pillars of the strategy
The DDPS structures the response on three main axes. First: the creation of a center for unmanned systems, ### How the drone systems center works
The new center integrates three crucial elements. The tech hub brings together the operational needs of the armed forces, the technological expertise of armasuisse (the federal armament agency), and knowledge from universities, startups and the private sector. The objective is to collaborate to develop, test and quickly deploy innovative solutions for military use.
The military command, on the other hand, manages an **organization for experimentation and training**: it tests new systems in realistic conditions and is responsible for training the drone battalion. A virtuous circle: the knowledge acquired by troops in the field is transmitted to the scientific and business world through the tech hub.
### Implications for the national defense system
The choice of shorter acquisition cycles and smaller quantities reflects the accelerated pace of technological innovation. The armed forces intend to acquire systems in a targeted manner, in short cycles, rapidly introducing what proves effective and developing it further based on acquired experience. This agile approach reduces the risks of technological obsolescence, a serious problem in the military sector due to the exponential progress of artificial intelligence and robotics.
For the system to function, seamless collaboration is required between institutional levels: federal, cantonal and private. The DDPS has provided that the center be accessible to other departments, cantons and emergency response organizations, expanding the public benefit of research and experimentation.
A parallel challenge concerns skills and legal bases in drone defense. Today this responsibility is fragmented among various public authorities and private infrastructure managers. An interdepartmental working group led by the DDPS is examining current competencies and evaluating necessary regulatory adjustments. Work is also proceeding following a parliamentary mandate (motion 25.4410), a sign of political interest in this critical issue.
### Opportunities for military careers and training
The establishment of a drone battalion and a dedicated recruit school opens new employment prospects within the Swiss armed forces. Personnel qualified in technology, robotics and artificial intelligence will have significant professional career opportunities. The DDPS also intends to benefit from the experience of militia personnel already active in the economic, scientific and technological sectors, creating bridges between the civil and Swiss military worlds. The drone battalion becomes operational starting in 2028, with the concurrent opening of the recruit school for drones. In the meantime, the 2027 armament program already provides specific funding to equip the new unit and strengthen drone defense systems.
Investments will not stop in 2028. The military will continue the systematic integration of drone expertise throughout the military structure, adopting a continuous learning approach based on operational data and experiences acquired in the field.
### The role of cantons and civil collaboration
Swiss cantons have a crucial role in defending against drone attacks, particularly those targeting critical regional infrastructure such as water and energy networks. The interdepartmental working group led by the DDPS is precisely defining who assumes which responsibility. This regulatory clarification is urgent: current ambiguities over competencies could create operational gaps in case of real crisis.

The Federal Council responded to a motion by National Councillor Thomas de Courten (UDC/BS) calling for the abolition of the sticky motorway vignette. The decision is clear: the adhesive version will remain available for several more years, despite the growing preference for the electronic one.
The adhesive vignette involves considerable costs related to production, distribution, sales and accounting. An exclusively electronic system would represent an annual saving of about 20 million francs — given that it fueled Courten's motion. However, the Swiss Parliament opted for a dual system. ### The dynamics of the digital transition
The 50% share of electronic vignettes planned for 2026 represents an important reference point on the path towards the abolition of the adhesive version. However, the Government does not specify a precise date to reach 10%, limiting itself to observing that it will have to wait "several more years". The exact timeline will depend on the speed with which Swiss motorists will spontaneously adopt the digital mark.
In parallel, Austria will proceed with the total elimination of the sticker vignette from 2027. This creates an asymmetrical scenario: those who move between Switzerland and Austria will have freedom of choice on the one hand (Switzerland) and will be obliged to go digital on the other (Austria). The saving of about CHF 20 million per year is a considerable figure in the budget of the Federal Administration. item.description: RT.DE and social media used by Moscow to influence the September 27 neutrality vote. Government acknowledges threat of disinformation.

## In a nutshell - Vote on neutrality on September 27, 2026 - Kremlin uses RT.DE and social media to influence campaign - Federal Government Recognizes Growing Threat of Foreign Disinformation
## Key facts - **What**: Constitutional initiative on neutrality with prohibition of sanctions against states in armed conflict - When: Vote on September 27, 2026 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Kremlin, media RT.DE, SEPOS, Federal Council - Opposition: Federal Council opposes the initiative - Source: SRF reports on the influence operation
The Kremlin has repeatedly tried to influence the campaign on Swiss neutrality in recent weeks, SRF reported. Swiss citizens will vote on the initiative on 27 September 2026. The proposal would write into the Swiss constitution a broad ban on sanctions against states involved in armed conflict, with the exception of Switzerland's obligations to the United Nations.
### Moscow's campaign through the media
RT.DE, a Kremlin-funded newspaper, published several articles during the campaign. These articles were critical of the Federal Council, which opposes the initiative, and supportive of the proposal. Some of these articles are attributed to Hans-Ueli Läppli, although no journalist by this name can be identified. The surname is familiar in Switzerland from Alfred Rasser's fictional character, Theophil Läppli, a Swiss soldier ## # Expert analysis and normalization strategy
Ulrich Schmid, professor of Eastern European studies at the University of St. Gallen, explained the significance of the Kremlin campaign to SRF. The Kremlin is trying to present the war in Ukraine as an ordinary two-state conflict. Adding neutrality to the Swiss constitution would play into the hands of the Kremlin, normalizing the conflict. Schmid predicts that such influence efforts will likely have little direct effect on Swiss voters' choices. However, he stresses that Switzerland should still take them seriously, as attempts to influence Swiss public opinion are part of a much broader Kremlin strategy of destabilization. This strategy is designed to operate in the long term, according to the scholar's analysis.
## # Federal Government Recognition and SEPOS Warning
The federal government recognizes the problem. In response to a request from SRF, the State Secretariat for Security Policy (SEPOS) stated that foreign disinformation and state-funded influence attempts, specifically targeting Switzerland, are on the rise. In a draft security policy document, SEPOS warns that foreign influence operations and disinformation can directly affect the results of elections and referendums. Such campaigns aim to polarise societies and undermine trust in democratic institutions.

item.title: Canicola and drought: the Government wants more funds
item.description: The Federal Council is asking for CHF 71.5 million to support forests and farmers affected by the record drought of 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Government asks CHF 71.5 million for droughts and forests - CHF 17.5 million per year from 2027 for woodland adaptation - CHF 54 million in 2026 for cash-strapped farms - Record-low rainfall until mid-August 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Extraordinary federal funding for drought and agriculture - When: Discussion on Wednesday Federal Council; evaluation by the end of October, autumn decision - Where: Switzerland (Canton Zurich, Vaud, other affected regions) - Who: Federal Council; Parliament; DATEC, DEFR, DFI, DDPS - Amount: CHF 17.5 million forest credit 2027+ + CHF 54 million agriculture 2026 - Aid type: Interest-free receivables for liquidity - Sectors affected: Agriculture, forests, shipping, electricity
The Federal Council discussed on Wednesday the situation of heatwave and drought that is affecting Switzerland. The decision is clear: it calls on Parliament to allocate extraordinary funds to support farms and adapt forests to ongoing climate change.
The figures are significant. The executive calls for an increase of 17.5 million francs for forest credit in 2027. In addition, from 2028, the Federal Department of Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC) will be able to request funds of the same amount every year. For agriculture, the means rise by 54 million francs in 2026, as a one-off support for companies in liquidity crisis caused ### What Concretely Changes
The announced financing represents a break from the usual ordinary federal budget cycle. Normally, forest credit and agricultural aid follow standard and predictable paths of annual programming. This time, the Federal Council recognizes that the liquidity crisis for farmers is immediate and cannot wait for ordinary timelines. An emergency situation requires emergency tools.
The mechanism is simple from an operational standpoint: those who benefit are farmers affected by drought and public and private forest owners. How? Through bank credits guaranteed by the Confederation, interest-free. When? The 54 million for agriculture is already available in 2026; the 17.5 million for forests comes into force from 2027, with the possibility of annual renewal from 2028 onwards.
This means that a farm that has seen its harvests collapse, with emergency irrigation costs or livestock management costs drastically increased due to drought, can access these funds to maintain operational liquidity until the next production cycle. These are not direct aid (non-repayable subsidies), but subsidized financing that must be repaid. The absence of interest reduces the overall cost of the liquidity crisis.
### Implications for Affected Sectors
For agricultural enterprises, interest-free credit represents an essential injection of liquidity at a critical moment. The Confederation, through the cantons, supports agricultural enterprises to overcome the crisis without resorting to the ordinary credit market, where interest rates would be significantly higher and the availability of financing could be limited given the risk profile of the sector during periods of disaster.
For forests, the annual financing of 17.5 million (starting from 2027) allows cantons and owners to invest in concrete climate adaptation measures: emergency irrigation for young plants, selection and planting of drought-resistant forest species, prevention of wildfires through fuel reduction interventions. In Switzerland, forests are not purely private property: many belong to municipalities or cantons, and the public interest in keeping them healthy is evident from an economic and environmental perspective.
The subsequent expansion of annual appropriations (from 2028 the DATEC can request funds every year based on needs) suggests that the Government foresees a long-term situation, not an episodic one. The 2026 drought, with record-low precipitation until mid-August, may not be an isolated exception but a signal of structural climate change. For farmers, the 54 million francs allocated in 2026 are available through the ordinary channel of applying for concessional credit with cantonal administrations. Each canton has a specific office (usually the Department of Agriculture) responsible for managing these extraordinary funds. The agricultural enterprise in question must demonstrate concrete damage from drought — significantly reduced harvests, additional irrigation costs, livestock losses — and present a realistic financial repayment plan in order to access the credit.
The credit is interest-free, which means the enterprise repays only the principal borrowed, without any additional financial costs. This drastically reduces the cost of the crisis compared to an ordinary bank loan, where interest could absorb significant resources during the recovery period. The administrative procedure is streamlined compared to normal credit evaluation standards: there are no lengthy credit assessments, but rather a verification of the drought-related crisis situation.
For forest owners, the process is similar: the cantons make available 17.5 million annually (starting from 2027) through offices competent in forest management. The resources are intended for concrete adaptation projects — land reclamation, reforestation with resilient species, fire protection — which must be documented and authorized by the cantons before disbursement.
### What happens by October and autumn
The Government has set precise deadlines for following up on the situation. By the end of October, the federal departments DATEC, DEFR, DFI, and DDPS will complete a new in-depth analysis of the drought, energy, and agriculture situation. If the drought continues or other related crises emerge (for example, risks to hydroelectric energy production due to critical water levels in dams, river navigation problems, further agricultural losses), the Government could propose additional support measures.
In autumn (September–November 2026), the Federal Council will make a final decision on any new interventions that go beyond the already announced package of 71.5 million. This means that those awaiting a definitive response from the Government on additional measures should know that the most important decisions will come in the coming months of autumn 2026. In the meantime, cantonal administrations will be able to begin collecting applications and processing agricultural credit requests based on the 54 million allocated for 2026.
### Next operational steps
Those working in agriculture or owning forests in Switzerland should stay in contact with the competent cantonal office (Department of Agriculture or Forest) to understand how to access the funds and what the specific procedures are. The allocated amounts, application timelines, and conditions vary from canton to canton, although federal financing is coordinated at the central level by DATEC and departmental partners.
If you work in the agricultural sector or in areas related to climate resilience, [consult Swiss job listings](nav:jobs) for opportunities at companies investing in adaptation and sustainability. item.description: Federal administration: surplus of 4 billion in 2025, gross debt rises to 353.2 billion (40.7% GDP). Impact on taxes and social benefits.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Public budget surplus of approximately 4 billion CHF in 2025 - Gross public debt rises to 353.2 billion CHF (40.7% of GDP) - Data published August 27, 2026 by the Federal Administration
## Key Facts - **What**: Aggregated Swiss public budget - When: Year 2025, published August 27, 2026 - Where: Switzerland (Confederation, Cantons, Municipalities, social insurance) - Who: Federal Finance Administration - Surplus: approximately 4 billion CHF - Gross debt: 353.2 billion CHF - Debt-to-GDP ratio: 40.7%
The Federal Finance Administration has released new financial statistics data for 2025. Overall, all Swiss public administrations — Confederation, Cantons, Municipalities, and social insurance — should record a financing surplus of approximately 4 billion francs. However, the picture becomes more complex when looking at total debt: gross public debt, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) definition, should increase in 2025 by approximately 5.4 billion francs.
The result is that Swiss gross public debt will reach 353.2 billion francs, equivalent to 40.7 percent of national gross domestic product. This means that for every 100 francs of wealth produced by the Swiss economy, public debt represents 40.7 francs — a measure of fiscal sustainability crucial for assessing the financial health of the country.
Data published by the Federal Finance Administration website includes three levels of detail: data from the 'Main Groups', 'Detailed SF Data' (financial statistics, with comparability at the national level) and 'Detailed GFS Data' (Government Finance Statistics, based on IMF international standards). An 'International Comparison' is also available to place Swiss budgets in a global context.
### What it means for taxpayers The public budget surplus is generally a positive sign for Swiss taxpayers, as it indicates that tax revenues — derived from federal direct tax, VAT, and cantonal and municipal taxes — exceed current spending. However, the simultaneous increase in gross public debt suggests that much of this wealth ends up in long-term financing mechanisms, often linked to public investments, welfare programs (AVS, LPP, LAMal benefits) and infrastructure.
Even if 2025 data shows an overall surplus, this does not necessarily mean that federal, cantonal, or municipal taxes will decrease. In the short term, the surplus could be allocated to pay off previous debts or to finance new social programs (AVS, LPP, LAMal). Anyone who resides or works in Switzerland should verify how this fiscal situation affects their [income tax return](nav:tax-return).
The volatility between annual surplus and debt accumulation illustrates how Swiss fiscal management follows long-term sustainability logic, not perfect annual balance. For this reason, taxpayers should not expect drastic fiscal decisions based on single budget years, but rather monitor the multi-year guidelines of the Federal Council and cantonal governments. Practical analysis: the coexistence of surplus and growing debt
The coexistence of a budget surplus and growing debt may seem contradictory, but it reflects a financial reality common to developed countries. Surplus represents the net balance between current receipts and outflows in a year, while gross debt is the stock accumulated over time by public liabilities — including loans, government debt securities, and future obligations towards welfare programs.
### Distribution of debt among levels of government Switzerland's 353.2 billion gross public debt is not concentrated at the federal level. The Federal Finance Administration provides a cross-analysis showing how the debt burden is distributed among the Confederation, Cantons and Municipalities. Each level of government has its own fiscal autonomy — each canton sets its own cantonal tax rates within federal limits, and each municipality sets its own municipal multiplier on a cantonal basis.
This means that fiscal sustainability varies greatly from Canton to Canton. A Canton like Zurich or Geneva may have very different debt and surplus profiles than Ticino or Appenzell.
