item.title: US duty reimbursement: administrative fear
item.description: Only a third of Swiss companies ask for reimbursement of improperly collected US duties. The others give up for fear of excessive administrative burdens.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Only 1/3 of Swiss companies request reimbursement of improperly collected US tariffs - They fear administrative costs exceeding financial gains - Online form available, but Swissmem should promote it better - Expected decline in overseas business activity for most companies
## Key facts - **What**: Reimbursement of US tariffs on machinery, electronics, metals sector - Who: Swissmem (Swiss industry association), Martin Hirzel (president) - Percentage of applicants: Only 1/3 of companies have requested reimbursement - Main obstacle: Fear of administrative costs vs. modest financial gain - Procedure: Online form available but 'rather complicated' - Communication: Swissmem does not adequately promote the procedure - Outlook: Majority of companies expect declining activity in the United States
Only one-third of Swiss companies active in the machinery, electronics, and metals sector have requested reimbursement from the United States for improperly collected tariffs. This was revealed by Martin Hirzel, president of the industry association Swissmem, in an interview with financial agency AWP. This data illuminates a significant discrepancy: two out of three companies formally forgo recovering amounts owed, despite the right being established and the procedure being technically accessible.
The reasons for this massive abstention are primarily administrative. Companies fear excessive bureaucratic costs in the face of modest financial gain. This creates a scenario in which the perceived cost of the request exceeds the expected benefit, discouraging action.
### The procedural transparency issue
Hirzel openly acknowledges that companies must fill out a 'rather complicated' form, although the procedure can be completed online. The paradox is evident: the digital channel exists, but the perception of complexity hinders participation. More significantly, the president does not exclude the association's own responsibility: 'Perhaps Swissmem should also promote this procedure more clearly', he stated.
This admission reveals a communication gap. If Swissmem could offer transparent guidance, support in document collection, and specific training on form completion, the participation rate would presumably increase. The gap between formal right and actual exercise is thus bridgeable, but requires active advocacy from the industry association.
In the broader context, companies have 'learned to coexist with customs tariffs', according to Hirzel. However, the distance from normalizing the commercial situation with the United States remains real. Tariff volatility and continual regulatory adjustments keep companies in a state of permanent adaptation. Those wishing to delve deeper into the tax implications of international business operations can consult [resources on tax returns and compliance](nav:tax-return). The administrative burden resulting from tariffs and constantly changing regulations exerts direct pressure on the profitability and operational capacity of companies. Companies do not only face the immediate economic problem of tariffs, but also the hidden costs associated with compliance, management of international documentation, and continuous updating of internal processes.
A concrete consequence is the uncertainty transmitted to international customers. American buyers of Swiss products in the machinery, electronic components, and metal goods sectors operate in a precarious situation. Profit margins remain uncertain, delivery times undergo variations due to administrative obstacles, final prices remain exposed to tariff volatility. This creates a spiral of risks that discourages volume orders and long-term contracts.
### Predictions of Contraction and Communication Failure
The majority of interviewed Swissmem companies predict a decline in overseas activity. This is not a marginal forecast: the American market remains strategic for the Swiss precision industry. A widespread contraction in exports to the USA would entail cascading repercussions on employment, research and development investments, and overall sector competitiveness.
The problem of inadequate communication emerges clearly from Hirzel's statement. If the reimbursement procedure remains poorly known and underutilized, the economic loss for companies accumulates over time, year after year. This is not a single recovery, but a series of missed reimbursements that progressively erode operating margins and investment capacity.
Constantly changing regulations further amplify the damage. Every change in customs rules or tariff rates entails the need for internal updates, staff training, and process revision. For small and medium-sized companies, these administrative costs can be significant and difficult to absorb, especially if they simultaneously lose market share due to tariff instability. Companies thus find themselves trapped in a cycle of increasing administrative costs facing increasingly uncertain revenues.
For those operating in the international commercial field and needing to understand currency dynamics in real time, [the CHF/EUR exchange rate comparator provides current data](nav:exchange).
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). Companies interested in recovering duties improperly collected have access to a formal procedure with the American customs authorities. Although the form is complex, online filing remains the only effective way to recover the amounts owed and should not discourage initiative. The first operational step is to contact the American customs authorities (U.S. Customs and Border Protection) directly, or to contact Swissmem to obtain initial informational support on the procedure and required documentation.
The procedure requires: precise identification of duties paid in excess; collection of commercial documentation (invoices, licenses, certificates of origin, original customs declarations); accurate completion of the specific form according to American criteria. Although the process can be completed online, it is essential to devote sufficient time to collecting documentation and verifying data accuracy. Procedural errors result in rejection of the request and loss of the right to reimbursement.
### How to proceed effectively
Swissmem could develop a crucial role in providing technical assistance to members: step-by-step guides, training webinars on completion, referrals to customs tariff experts, standardized document templates. Currently, President Hirzel has explicitly acknowledged that this support function is insufficient. Companies proceeding independently must nevertheless evaluate the cost-benefit: if the expected reimbursement is less than CHF 5,000–10,000 (not specified in the source, but realistic for average amounts), spending on external consulting could erode the entire net gain.
A strategic element is timing. Duty recovery is not immediate and requires administrative patience and following specific procedures. Interested companies must proceed without delay, as there are presumably time limits for claims under American regulations (although not explicitly stated in Hirzel's communication).
Furthermore, exporting companies should comprehensively evaluate their commercial strategy towards the USA in a strategic perspective. If customs regulations remain unstable and administrative costs high, geographic diversification of markets, reconsideration of price margins, or negotiation of contracts with tariff adjustment clauses could prove strategic. ## Key facts - **What**: Federal allocation of CHF 73 million to mitigate effects of summer 2026 drought - When: Announced on August 27, 2026 during federal press conference - Where: Federal level (Federal Council, DATEC) - Who: Albert Rösti (federal councillor), Lisa Mazzone (Greens president), Jürg Grossen (Green Liberals president) - Amount: CHF 73 million total (CHF 54 M agriculture + CHF 17.5 M forests) - Period: Forest funds guaranteed until 2031
The Federal Council is allocating 73 million francs to mitigate the effects of summer drought. This is announced by federal councillor Albert Rösti, head of the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DATEC), during a press conference in which he responds to criticism over alleged slowness in responding to the heat wave.
In the package of measures, the Government allocates 54 million francs to farmers, as compensation for loss of income caused by drought. An additional credit of 17.5 million finances forests until 2031, reintroducing funds previously cut in the federal savings package. For the rest, the Confederation has tasked a roundtable with offices and experts to identify additional needs by the end of October and propose any further measures.
Rösti defends the Federal Council's climate policy as a result of political compromises. The Confederation, he emphasizes, already spends 115 million francs per year on forests. To which are added the 17.5 million announced today, a figure set to double with cantonal contributions. These funds are not limited to 2027, but guaranteed until 2031. More broadly, the Confederation invests approximately 3 billion francs in global climate measures: climate protection, decarbonization, abandonment of fossil fuels, protection of biodiversity and adaptation to climate change.

But for the rest, it doesn't get to the root of the problem: no measures for cities, health, the population... nothing'. Different is the position of the Green Liberals: their president Jürg Grossen states: 'What is being proposed today is insufficient, the response is also too slow, but it is something. We will support these measures'.

All measures that, however, require time. For Swiss farmers, the compensation of CHF 54 million represents a concrete recognition of the damages suffered. item.title: Graubünden: property tax on second homes from 2029
item.description: The Government of Grison proposes a tax of 1.5‰ on secondary homes to compensate for losses of CHF 40.5 million. Population will vote on constitutional change.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell
- Grisioni abolishes rental value tax on second homes for own use - Estimated losses: CHF 40.5 million/year canton, 32.4 million common - New proposed rate: 1.5‰ on the tax value of the property - Expected validity: 1 January 2029 if approved by popular vote
## Key facts
- **What**: Abolition of rental value tax, introduction of new property tax on second homes - When: Effective from 1 January 2029 (if popular vote approves) - Where: Canton of Graubünden (eastern Switzerland) - Who: Government of Grison - Canton amount: Loss CHF 40.5 million per year to be compensated - Common amount: Loss CHF 32.4 million per year - Proposed rate: 1.5 per thousand on the tax value
### Announcement by the Grayish government
The government of the canton of Graubünden has announced a significant tax reform: the abolition of the rental value tax for secondary homes for own use, offset by a new property tax. The decision will result in a budget loss of approximately CHF 40.5 million per year for the canton, a considerable amount that requires rapid compensatory action.
To cope with this reduction in income, the cantonal executive proposes the introduction of a special real estate tax calculated on the tax value of the real estate substance with a rate of 1.5 per thousand. According to the government statement, this rate represents the minimum parameter deemed necessary to compensate for losses in ## Analysis of the national fiscal impact
This Grisonese reform represents a significant paradigm shift in cantonal real estate taxation. The loss of CHF 40.5 million for the canton and CHF 32.4 million for the municipalities amounts to a real redistribution of the tax burden towards the real estate sector, with a specific focus on owners of second homes. In the general context of Swiss public funding, where the cantons independently manage their taxation, this represents one of the most important structural changes in recent years.
The proposed rate of 1.5 per thousand, although formally contained, will have concrete effects on those who own secondary properties in Graubünden. A homeowner with a tax value of CHF 1 million would pay CHF 1,500 in tax annually. On mid-range properties (600,000-800,000 francs), the amount would be between 900 and 1,200 francs per year. This represents a fixed additional cost in addition to ordinary income taxation and other cantonal and municipal taxes.
### Municipal differentiation and strategic implications
The government's decision to grant municipalities full autonomy in adopting (or waiving) the tax creates a two-speed system within the canton. Wealthy and well-funded municipalities may decide not to introduce the tax, remaining competitive to attract real estate investments and second-hand owners ## What Changes from January 1, 2029
If the popular vote approves the constitutional amendment, starting from January 1, 2029, owners of secondary residences for personal use in the canton of Grisons will transition from an imputed rental value tax regime (calculated on the assumed income of the property) to a flat-rate tax based exclusively on the tax value of the real estate asset, with a minimum rate of 1.5 per mille.
Individual municipalities will be able to adopt their own rates within this system, with the possibility of setting percentages higher or lower than 1.5‰, or opting out entirely. This variability makes it essential for the owner to verify the specific decisions of the municipality where the secondary property is located, not the municipality of principal residence.
### Concrete Procedure for Owners
If you own a second home in Grisons, the steps to follow in the coming months and years are:
1. Monitor the outcome of the popular vote (date not yet announced, expected sometime between late 2026 and early 2027 according to the canton's legislative timeline) 2. Contact the municipality where the property is located to learn the local decision regarding the tax on second homes 3. **Request formal clarification** on: applicable local rate, method for calculating the tax value, payment procedures (annual, semi-annual, quarterly installments), deadlines for filing property tax returns 4. Update your overall tax planning by including the new liability in evaluating the total cost of ownership 5. Optionally consult a tax adviser specializing in cantonal taxation to optimize your overall tax situation
### Timeline for Purchases and Planning
Anyone considering purchasing a secondary property in Grisons has a limited time window before 2029. If the acquisition takes place by December 2028, the property will be subject to the old tax regime for at least part of 2029. However, the real probability of approval by the population makes it prudent to include the new tax liability in your economic feasibility assessments today.
An owner purchasing a home for 750,000 Swiss francs in 2028 should expect an additional annual cost of approximately 1,125 Swiss francs (750,000 × 0.0015) starting from 2029, increasing the total cost of managing the property. This parameter must be factored into the ROI (return on investment) calculation of the real estate transaction.
### Tax Declaration and Administrative Compliance
From 2029 onward, owners of real estate in Grisons will need to include the new real estate tax item in their cantonal tax returns. The dynamics will be similar to other cantonal and municipal taxes, with official communications from the canton guiding the procedures for filing and payment deadlines. It is likely that the canton will issue a separate tax notice for this new tax, distinct from the ordinary income tax.
For those managing complex real estate portfolios or owning multiple secondary properties in different areas of Switzerland (for example in both Grisons and Valais or Ticino), this change represents an opportunity to review your overall wealth allocation strategy and assess whether to keep, sell, or acquire properties based on the new tax regime.
### Stay Updated on Cantonal Tax Reforms
Swiss cantonal tax changes are frequent and sometimes complex. To stay informed about how decisions like the Grisons decision affect your property and tax situation, consult our [tax return guide](nav:tax-return) and sign up to receive updates on tax changes in Switzerland. Understanding in advance the impact of new taxes on your property enables you to plan more effectively.

item.title: Credible neutrality requires an active role
item.description: Historian Matthieu Gillabert analyzes how the doctrine of Swiss neutrality has evolved, to understand the active role necessary for its credibility.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Contemporary Swiss neutrality requires active participation in international politics - Historian Matthieu Gillabert explores the evolution of the doctrine of neutrality - Credibility of neutrality depends on engagement in international institutions
## Key facts - **Topic**: Swiss foreign policy and the evolution of neutrality - Protagonist: Historian Matthieu Gillabert - Central concept: Credible neutrality and active role - Context: Federal institutions and international relations - Implication: Active participation in world affairs
Swiss foreign policy faces a fundamental contemporary challenge: how to maintain credibility in neutrality while taking an increasingly active role in international affairs. This is the central theme of a historical analysis conducted by historian Matthieu Gillabert, which examines how and for what reasons the guiding doctrine of Swiss neutrality has evolved.
The title of this reflection — “Credible neutrality requires an active role” — sums up a powerful idea: Switzerland cannot maintain its neutrality by withdrawing from the world. On the contrary, the credibility of neutrality depends on the way in which the country actively participates in international decision-making processes, from multilateral organizations to diplomatic negotiations.
For decades, Swiss neutrality has been interpreted as a position of non-alignment and The idea of an 'active neutrality' reflects how Switzerland has reconciled the apparent contradiction between traditional non-alignment and participation in multilateral institutions. In the contemporary context, a purely passive position is no longer sustainable in the face of global challenges and the need for international credibility.
Swiss federal institutions must therefore navigate a delicate balance. On one hand, they maintain the historical commitment to neutrality. On the other, they recognize that the absence of a voice in international decision-making processes would threaten the very credibility that neutrality intends to preserve.
This balance manifests itself in various ways. Switzerland participates in diplomatic negotiations, adheres to international agreements while always maintaining the possibility of staying outside formal alliances, and contributes to humanitarian and peacekeeping efforts. Every action is calculated to strengthen the prestige of Swiss neutrality rather than weaken it.
### The Importance of Credibility in Neutrality
A neutrality that is not backed by an active commitment to seeking solutions to global problems risks being perceived as indifference rather than principle. Gillabert's research contributes to explaining how Switzerland has historically built credibility through concrete actions — from mediation in international conflicts to the provision of humanitarian services — rather than through simple declarations of neutrality.
For Swiss citizens and for those who live or work in the country, this evolution of the doctrine of neutrality has direct implications. It determines how the country relates to its trading partners, how it participates in negotiations on economic and security issues, and what influence it exercises in defining international norms.
Neutrality, in this sense, is not a purely abstract concept of foreign policy. It is a strategic choice that influences the value of the [Swiss franc in the global market](nav:exchange), its reputation as an international mediator, and its capacity to attract investment and talent from abroad.

The Swiss Federal Council regularly publishes reports and documents on foreign policy, available through official channels of the federal administrations. These materials provide insights into strategic decisions and the principles that guide them.

Interested citizens can follow these proceedings to understand how their representatives address global challenges. Swiss national media also regularly cover foreign policy decisions, offering analysis and commentary.
### Why This Matters for Switzerland
Foreign policy is not confined to diplomatic debate. Decisions about how Switzerland positions itself internationally directly affect citizens:
- **Trade Relations**: International trading partners consider Switzerland's stability and reputation when deciding to do business with the Country. - Economic Stability: Credible neutrality contributes to confidence in global markets and Switzerland's attractiveness as a financial hub. - Employment Opportunities: An active role for Switzerland in international institutions creates employment opportunities in the public sector and in international organizations based in Switzerland. - Security: Foreign policy decisions influence Switzerland's national security and stability in the European geopolitical context.

item.title: Residence permit C St. Gallen: requirements and application

item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit C: permanent residence after 10 years (5 EU/EFTA years) - Valid for 5 years, renewable, subject to integration - Issued by canton and municipality upon verification of requirements - Does not require work motivations
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit C (permanent residence in Switzerland) - When: After a minimum of 10 years of residence (5 years EU/EFTA citizens) - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, request at the municipal office - Who: Foreign citizens who respect residence and integration - Validity: 5 years renewable with integration assessment
The C permit represents the official recognition of the right of permanent residence in Switzerland. Unlike the B permit (residence, temporary and renewable on an employment or family basis), the C permit is not subject to the maintenance of a working activity and offers long-term legal stability for those who intend to reside permanently in the canton of St. Gallen.
According to federal regulations on residence, the C permit is normally issued after the completion of 10 years of uninterrupted residence in the Swiss territory. Citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) — Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — benefit from a shortened path: a legal residence of 5 years is sufficient for them.
The issuance of the C permit is not automatic. Even after having completed the required years of residence, the cantonal administration and the ### Integration criteria in the canton of St. Gallen
Civil and economic integration is the cornerstone on which the issuance and renewal of the C permit is based. Cantonal and municipal administrations do not require the adoption of Swiss citizenship or total cultural conformity, but rather respect for the laws, the capacity for self-support and constructive participation in the life of the community.
The integration criteria generally considered include:
- **Knowledge of the language**: ability to communicate in German (official language of the canton of St. Gallen) at the level of daily conversation with public institutions and in civic life. The cantons and the Confederation do not set a mandatory CEFR level, but the authorities carry out a practical assessment of communicative competence. - Legal situation: absence of significant criminal convictions or violations of public order, timely submission of [dichiarazione d'imposta](nav:tax-return), regular payment of social contributions ([AVS/LPP](nav:pension)), payment of [assicurazione malattia LAMal](nav:health) taxes. - Economic self-support: demonstration of a stable source of income (employment, self-employment, pension, real estate income) and timely payment of federal, cantonal and municipal taxes. - Social integration: constructive participation in the local community, no reports to the authorities, no financial burden on public coffers.
### EU/EFTA vs. third-country nationals
EU citizens and ### How to Apply for Permit C in the Canton of St. Gallen
The procedures described below represent the typical process; specific details may vary slightly between municipalities in the Canton of St. Gallen. It is recommended to contact the relevant municipal office in advance to verify local procedures.
Phase 1: Verification of Residence Prerequisites
Before applying, ensure that the residence requirements have been fully met: - EU and EFTA citizens: minimum 5 years of continuous legal residence in Switzerland. - Third-country citizens: minimum 10 years of continuous legal residence in Switzerland.
Residence must be documented through valid residence permits (short-term L permits or B residence permits) issued by Swiss authorities, or equivalent documents certifying legal presence in the territory.
Phase 2: Verification of Compliance with Integration Criteria
Before submitting your application, verify that you meet the essential requirements: - Absence of serious criminal convictions or ongoing criminal proceedings. - Regular and timely payment of [AVS/AI/IPG](nav:pension) contributions through your employer (if employed) or via voluntary payment (if self-employed or retired). - Timely payment of federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes, with no tax arrears. - Enrollment in a [health insurance fund (LAMal/KVG)](nav:health) with regular premium payments. - Ability to communicate in German at an elementary level in daily life.
Phase 3: Preparation of Required Documentation
The exact documents vary according to your municipality of residence, but generally include: - Official application form for Permit C (available at the municipal office or downloadable from the cantonal administration website). - Valid identity document (national passport, identity card, previous residence permits). - Current residence certificate. - Tax documentation for the past 3–5 years, confirming timely tax payments. - Certificate or confirmation of [AVS](nav:pension) contribution payments issued by your employer or the relevant AVS office. - Confirmation of current employment status (valid employment contract, self-employed certificate, pension decision from the disability insurance office). - In case of criminal records in the country of origin, statement of no conviction or equivalent administrative certificate.
**Phase 4: Submission of Application**
The application must be submitted to the municipal office of the locality where the applicant resides in the Canton of St. Gallen. This is the first point of administrative contact. The municipal office will subsequently transmit the application to the cantonal migration office if necessary for final evaluation.
There is no strict deadline for submitting the application, but it is advisable to submit it promptly after completing 5 or 10 years of residence, to avoid administrative backlogs that could prolong processing times.
Phase 5: Administrative Review and Outcome
Processing the application typically takes several months. During this period, the competent authorities: - Verify the completeness and accuracy of the documentation provided. - Consult records with the cantonal police and municipal authorities to ensure the applicant has no criminal records or relevant alerts. - Conduct an overall assessment of the level of civic and economic integration. - May request clarifications, additional documents, or invite you to informational interviews.
If the assessment is positive, Permit C is issued and sent to the applicant. The document is valid for 5 years from issuance and must be kept carefully, as it serves as an identity and travel document for entering and exiting Switzerland.
### After Receiving Permit C
Once in possession of Permit C, the holder enjoys a stable and permanent legal status. The document must always be kept at hand, stored securely (like a passport and identity card), and used as a travel document within and outside Switzerland.
For those wishing to proceed toward ordinary Swiss naturalization, Permit C is an indispensable prerequisite. The law requires at least 10 years of total residence in Switzerland (although some cantons and municipalities may recognize earlier periods with favorable assessment as 'double' up to a maximum of 18 years), as well as current possession of Permit C and meeting specific cantonal and municipal requirements.
To learn more about the exact procedures of your municipality of residence in Canton St. Gallen, consult the official website of the municipal administration or contact the migration office directly. If your application involves complex or controversial elements, you may also consult a law firm specializing in immigration and residence law.
To monitor your tax and contribution status during the process, regularly check the [tax return](nav:tax-return) and [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to ensure that your payments fully comply with Swiss regulations.

## Key facts - **What**: Tax system at three levels (federal, cantonal, municipal) - Where: Canton of St. Gallen - How: Progressive rates on taxable income with deductions allowed by law - Multipliers: Each municipality applies its own multiplier on cantonal tax - Declaration: Annual obligation with deadlines of the cantonal tax administration
The Swiss tax system is divided into three distinct levels: the direct federal tax administered by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA), the cantonal tax set by the legislation of each canton, and the municipal tax calculated by applying a multiplier to the cantonal rate. In the Canton of St. Gallen, as in the other 25 Swiss cantons, this composite system allows a distribution of the tax burden among the three levels of government.
Cantonal taxes in the Canton of St. Gallen follow a progressive rate on taxable income. Individuals residing in the canton are obliged to complete an annual [dichiarazione fiscale](nav:tax-return) indicating income, deductible expenses and other income. The cantonal law of St. Gallen defines ### From determining taxable income to progressive rates
In the Canton of St. Gallen, taxable income is calculated starting from gross income (wages, annuities, professional income) and subtracting all deductions allowed by cantonal law. The resulting taxable income is subject to a rate that varies progressively according to the income brackets: the higher the income, the higher the rate. This progressive system ensures that the tax burden is not proportional but increases as income grows.
Deductions allowed by Swiss law include mandatory contributions (AVS, AI, IPG) and deductions on a cantonal basis such as insurance expenses (sickness, accidents, civil liability), interest on mortgage debts, voluntary contributions in the form of [previdenza privata del terzo pilastro 3a](nav:pillar3) up to the annual ceilings, investment losses and other items defined by the cantonal law of St. Gallen.
### Impact of municipal multipliers on the overall tax burden
Once the cantonal tax administration calculates the cantonal tax on the basis of the cantonal rate and taxable income, the municipality of residence applies its own multiplier, determining the total municipal tax. Two St. Gallen citizens with the same taxable income may pay different municipal taxes if they reside in municipalities with different multipliers. This mechanism reflects the principle of Swiss fiscal federalism: autonomy

Filing a tax return in the Canton of St. Gallen can be done by following these main steps:
1. Gather income documents: salary certificates (for employees), pension certificates, professional income documents, social security certificates.

3. Indicate deductions: enter all permitted deductions (insurance premiums, pension contributions, mortgage interest) with supporting documentation.
4. Verify the calculation: check that the taxable income, the applicable tax rates, and the calculated tax are correct.
5. Submit the declaration: via the online portal (preferably) or by mail to the deadline indicated by the cantonal tax administration.
### Deadlines and Filing Deadline
The tax administration of the Canton of St. Gallen announces the filing deadlines annually for the [tax return](nav:tax-return). It is important to respect these deadlines to avoid administrative penalties. If taxes are owed, payment must be made according to the methods and deadlines specified by the tax administration.

The tax administration of the Canton of St. Gallen provides an online portal where you can: - Complete the declaration in digital format - Attach documents and receipts for deductions - Check the status of your previous declaration - View current tax rates and brackets for the current year - Download paper forms, if necessary

### The Swiss inheritance tax system
In Switzerland, the taxation of successions and donations is the exclusive responsibility of the cantons. The amount of the inheritance or donation affects the calculation. The tax base also varies depending on whether there are deductions, reductions in value or specific exemptions according to cantonal legislation.

Phase 4: Valuation of inherited assets Movable and immovable assets must be valued at market value or cadastral value according to cantonal regulations. Some assets may benefit from value reductions if subject to liens, usufruct, or other limitations.

The Inner Appenzell canton, like the other 25 cantons of the Swiss Confederation, structures its labour market around three complementary economic sectors. The primary sector (agriculture, forestry) represents a historical component of the Alpine region, although with limited employment compared to past decades. The secondary sector (textiles, machinery, construction, manufacturing) remains significant, a legacy of the ## Training and impact on net wages: practical scenarios The leverage of training broadly determines the net income received. A worker who completes only compulsory schooling accesses unskilled positions (general auxiliary, unskilled worker, basic clerk): the gross salary is the lowest. However, any Swiss salary — regardless of level — is subject to the same federal contributions in percentage (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, mandatory LAMal, LPP if contracted) and federal/cantonal/municipal taxes. It follows that the net is approx. 55–65% of the gross for low incomes, because the fixed percentages affect more heavily. An apprentice who completes the AFC (16–19 years old) enters the market as a technician, skilled worker, craftsman, experienced salesman. The gross salary is higher than the unqualified because the qualification is federally recognized and is transportable between companies and cantons. The same amount of federal contributions (5.3% AVS, 1.1% AD/AC) continues to apply, but the basis of calculation is higher; consequently the absolute net increases, although the deduction percentage remains the same. In addition, the employer has an incentive to keep the employee qualified. Those who attend a specialized school (technicum, business school, nursing school) reach an intermediate level: advanced technical skills without a full academic degree. Access locations of These contracts establish: minimum wage by degree of qualification and seniority, annual salary steps, Christmas bonuses, 13th month, reduced hours, days of continuous training. Even in Inner Appenzello, if you work in a sector covered by national CCL (e.g. bank, manufacturing industry adhering to a federal contract), the collective agreement applies automatically. Job search in Switzerland follows standardized procedures, applicable also in Appenzell Innerrhoden. The main job listing platforms are: [job.ch](nav:jobs), indeed.ch, linkedin.com (geographic filter "Switzerland"), swisstalents.ch for academic profiles. Many employers publish directly on their corporate websites. In the public sector (cantonal administration, municipalities, public hospitals), announcements are on the official public administration portal.
### ### Step-by-step: from search to first paycheck
Step 1: Define the sought profile Choose the sector (primary, secondary, tertiary) and the level of education required (compulsory schooling, apprenticeship, specialized school, university). Consult the [job announcement databases](nav:jobs) in your sector and with the desired qualification level.
Step 2: Assess the gross salary offered Many Swiss job listings indicate the salary range (e.g., "CHF 4500–5500/month gross"). If not specified, consult official sources: - UST/BFS (Federal Statistical Office, bfs.admin.ch): Official statistics of average salaries by economic sector, education level, sector, age group. These are the national reference data. - [Salary Calculator](nav:calculator): Enter the offered gross salary and instantly obtain the net amount, deductions, taxes, LAMal estimate, LPP. - SECO: The federal labor agency maintains guidelines on working conditions and wages by sector.
Step 3: Calculate net salary Net salary = gross – AVS/AI/IPG (5.3%) – AD/AC (1.1%, up to approx. CHF 148'000 gross annually) – direct federal tax – cantonal tax – municipal tax – LAMal (private insurance premium, not a deduction). LPP (second pillar) is a deduction only if the employment contract provides for it. Appenzell Innerrhoden, as a small alpine canton, generally has cantonal and municipal tax rates that are mid-low compared to urban cantons, which improves the relative net amount. Verify with the cantonal tax office the exact rate for your income.
For LAMal, compare health insurance funds with your profile (age, sex, canton, chosen deductible). Average premiums in 2026 range between CHF 200–350/month; Appenzell Innerrhoden generally has lower premiums than urban cantons.
Step 4: Review the employment contract Before signing, verify: - Term (fixed-term or indefinite) - Notice period (1 month during the first year, 2 months from the 2nd–9th year, 3 months from the 10th year onwards under federal law — the collective agreement cannot worsen these minimums) - Guaranteed vacation (minimum 4 weeks per year under federal law; 5 for those under 20 years old) - Maximum weekly working hours (45 hours for industry/offices/sales, 50 for other sectors) - LPP contributions: the employer must pay at least as much as the employee (often more), on coordinated salary (gross minus fixed coordination deduction) - Family allowances (if applicable; vary by canton and number of children) - Bonuses, 13th monthly salary, seniority increases (if collective agreement)
Step 5: Sign and provide banking details Sign the contract, provide your IBAN to the employer for salary deposit. The first paycheck arrives according to the company's payment schedule (usually end of month or every 15 days). Verify that the net matches your estimates.
### ### Tools and official online resources
For those entering the Swiss labor market or intending to relocate to Appenzell Innerrhoden:
SECO (seco.admin.ch): Federal guidelines on employment contracts, maximum working hours, worker rights, minimum wage by canton (if applicable), unemployment benefits, continuing education programs.
**UST/BFS** (bfs.admin.ch): Official statistical data on average salaries by sector, province, education level, gender, age group. Access "Work and Income" to download detailed tables.
Appenzell Innerrhoden Canton Portal: The cantonal administration publishes employment opportunities in the public sector, information on unemployment benefits, apprenticeship programs, tax incentives for education.

Health Insurance Comparator (Comparis, myCoverage): Compare LAMal premiums for your profile (age, sex, canton, deductible).
[Job Listing Portal](nav:jobs): Search open positions in Switzerland filtered by sector, canton, education level, contract type.
[Pension and Retirement Planning](nav:pension): Information on AVS/AHV, LPP/BVG, third pillar 3a. You can set aside up to CHF 35'280 annually (2026, indexed) in a 3a insurance policy with full tax deduction.
### ### Practical final advice
The key to navigating the Swiss labor market is understanding that gross salary ≠ net salary: federal contributions (AVS, AD/AC, LAMal, LPP) and cantonal/municipal taxes reduce the net by 30–45% depending on income and canton. Appenzell Innerrhoden, as a medium-sized alpine canton, offers a stable labor market with opportunities depending primarily on your qualification level and sector choice.
Before accepting a job offer, always simulate the net salary with the [official calculator](nav:calculator) and compare it with the local cost of living (rent, services, food, public transport). This way you will have a realistic view of your monthly purchasing power and can assess whether the offer is sustainable for your standard of living.

item.title: Lucerne naturalisation: 10 years and double counting
item.description: Permit C and 10 years of residency are the federal requirement. Periods between 8–18 years count double. Discover procedures, times and costs for naturalisation in Lucerne.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Ordinary naturalization requires a C permit and at least 10 years of residence in Switzerland - Periods between 8–18 years count double in the calculation of total residence - Each canton and municipality sets additional language, integration and duration requirements - Procedures and timing vary significantly between cantons and municipalities
## Key facts - **What**: Access to Swiss citizenship through ordinary naturalization - Who: Foreign holders of permit C (domicile) - Where: Procedures managed by municipal and cantonal authorities (including Lucerne) - Basic federal requirement: Permit C + 10 years of residence (with the possibility of double counting) - Double counting: Periods between 8–18 years of age multiplied by two for calculation purposes - Variable conditions: Language, integration, duration of cantonal/municipal residence (specific for canton Lucerne in the definition phase)
The federal regulatory framework states that anyone who holds a C permit (residence permit) and has resided in Switzerland for at least 10 years can apply for ordinary naturalization. However, this federal minimum requirement does not exhaust the process: each canton has the right to introduce stricter rules, and the same applies to the municipalities that administer the process at the territorial level.
Particularly relevant for those aspiring to ordinary naturalization is the double counting mechanism: periods of residence between 8 and 18 years of ## # Residence years accumulation mechanism
The residence counting system for the purposes of ordinary naturalization is structured according to the age of the resident: periods between 8 and 18 years old count twice, while all other periods (from birth to 8 years old and from 18 years old onwards) count once. The total required remains fixed at the federal level: 10 years equivalent.
A hypothetical scenario clarifies the mechanism: a person residing in Switzerland from the age of 15 to the age of 30 (15 linear years) accumulates residence calculated as follows: from 15 to 18 years = 3 years × 2 = 6 equivalent years; from 18 to 30 years = 12 years × 1 = 12 equivalent years; total = 18 equivalent years. This person reaches the threshold of 10 equivalent years before turning 30 thanks to the double counting bonus, despite having resided linearly for 15 years in Switzerland.
This mechanism has an important practical implication: it allows those who arrived in Switzerland during adolescence or early youth to accumulate the necessary years in less time than those who arrive later. A forty-year-old who moves to Switzerland will have all the years counted only once and will have to wait for the tenth year of actual residence; on the contrary, those who move at 15 will have an advantage in the calculation.
### Cantonal and municipal variable requirements
In addition to the federal requirement of 10 years residency (with double counting
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-Step Procedure for Ordinary Naturalization
The path towards ordinary naturalization follows standardized phases at the cantonal level, although with administrative variations from municipality to municipality.
Phase 1: Verification of Status and Prerequisites Before contacting the authorities, the candidate verifies their permit status (must be C, i.e., domicile permit) and calculates equivalent years of residence according to the double counting system for periods between 8–18 years. Residence is counted from the date of first settlement in Switzerland, regardless of the canton or municipality of initial arrival.
Phase 2: Contact with the Municipal Naturalization Office The candidate contacts the naturalization office of the municipality of residence to receive: the complete list of required documents (extracts from residence registers, certificates of non-registration in the criminal record, valid identity documents); specific language and integration requirements of Canton Lucerne and the municipality; information on municipal and cantonal fees; an estimate of the average duration of the procedure in the specific municipality.
Phase 3: Collection and Preparation of Documentation Typically required are: passport or valid identity document; recent residence certificate; criminal record certificate; proof of integration (employment contract, registrations in local associations, completion of language courses, certificates of civic participation); application form legally signed.
**Phase 4: Submission of Application** The formal application is submitted to the competent municipal authority. Some municipalities require a preliminary information meeting, an oral interview to verify knowledge of the cantonal language, or a presentation to the local community. This phase is fundamental because it establishes the official date of receipt of the application.
Phase 5: Verification by Cantonal Authority After submission to the municipality, the request is transmitted to the competent cantonal authority of Canton Lucerne. During this phase, integration requirements, knowledge of the language, complete documentation, and compliance with additional cantonal regulations are verified. The cantonal authority may request additional interviews or clarifications.
Phase 6: Decision and Formalization of Citizenship If approved, the decision is notified to the municipality, which communicates the result to the candidate. This is followed by official registration with the Civil Status Office and issuance of the naturalization certificate.
### Timeline, Costs and Next Steps
The overall duration of the procedure varies considerably between cantons and municipalities, on average requiring several months (typically from 6 to more than 12 months depending on the complexity of the case and the administrative workload of the municipality). Municipal and cantonal fees for ordinary naturalization vary significantly between different administrations. For specific values for Canton Lucerne and the municipality of residence, it is recommended to contact directly the competent municipal office during Phase 2.
Plan your naturalization path by first verifying the calculation of equivalent years of residence and then contacting the municipality. Furthermore, you can explore [employment opportunities in Switzerland](nav:jobs) to verify the occupational context during your integration path.

item.title: Family allowances Lucerne: amounts and procedure
item.description: How to apply for family allowances in Lucerne: who is entitled, monthly amounts per child, necessary documents and application procedure at the compensation fund.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Federal social benefit managed by the cantons with differentiated amounts per canton - Rights for employees, the self-employed and farmers with dependent children - Automatic monthly payment; application can be submitted at any time - Specific amounts 2026 available on the site of the canton Lucerne
## Key facts - **What**: Family and training allowances paid monthly for each dependent child - Where: Requested at the clearing house of the canton of Lucerne - Who: Employees, self-employed, farmers with dependent children, unemployed people with benefits - When: Application can be submitted at any time of the year; payment from month of approval - Cantons: 26 Swiss cantons, each with its own amounts set by law - System: Federal coordination, amounts and administrative management at cantonal level
Family allowances represent a social security benefit that Switzerland provides monthly to families for the support of dependent children. Unlike taxes and fees, family allowances constitute an economic transfer financed by the Swiss public system through a coordinated mechanism between the federal level and the cantons. In the canton of Lucerne, as in all 26 Swiss cantons, the right is recognized and regulated by law, but the specific monthly amounts for each child are determined by the canton itself according to its own rules.
This federal-cantonal structure ### Who is Entitled to Family Allowances in Lucerne
The right to family allowances in the canton of Lucerne is recognized for specific categories of people who engage in work activities or are in a situation of protection against unemployment. Those who can request the benefits include dependent workers (salaried employees) working in Lucerne, self-employed individuals and independent workers registered in the canton, as well as direct cultivators and farmers who exercise their activities in the Lucerne territory. Even people who are unemployed and receiving unemployment benefits can maintain the right to family allowances, although they are subject to specific criteria that vary by canton.
The fundamental element to access the benefit is the actual economic dependence of minors or young people in education or training. This means that the applicant must document that their children are effectively in their care from a financial point of view — that is, that they provide them with the main maintenance. For benefits extended to young people who continue their studies or professional training, the presentation of documents is required that certify the enrollment in an educational institution recognized by the competent authorities.
### Variability of Amounts Among Cantons
One of the most relevant aspects of the Swiss family allowance system is that the amounts are not uniform across the entire national territory. Each canton independently determines the amount it provides for the first child, for the second child, and for subsequent children, according to its own laws and regulations. Some cantons provide for progressive scales — that is, increasing amounts for subsequent children — while others maintain a fixed amount structure. The Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) collects and publishes comparative data on these amounts, allowing citizens to understand how their canton is positioned in the national landscape. Use our [cost of living comparator](nav:cost-of-living) to visualize how this differentiation between Swiss cantons is reflected in the different economic capacities of families.
To find out the exact amounts valid for the canton of Lucerne in the current year (2026), it is essential to consult the official tables published by the canton itself, generally available on the Lucerne canton website (www.lu.ch) in the section dedicated to social welfare and family allowances. These amounts are typically updated annually to account for the evolution of the cost of living and inflation; periodically checking any variations is advisable for all beneficiaries.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Request Procedure: How to Submit Your Application
The procedure for requesting family allowances in the canton of Lucerne follows a standardized and relatively simple path. The first step is to obtain the official application form, available from:
- The cantonal compensation fund of the canton of Lucerne - The municipality of residence - The canton of Lucerne's website in the section dedicated to family allowances
Once you have obtained the form, you must complete it with your personal data (name, surname, date of birth, AHV insurance number), the data of all dependent children for whom you are requesting the benefit (full names, dates of birth, school or training status if applicable), and your residence in the canton of Lucerne.
### Required Documents and Processing Times
The documents that accompany the application are essential for proper verification of eligibility. You must attach the following:
- Extract from the Civil Register for each dependent child (document attesting filiation and marital status) - Personal identity document (identity card, passport, or residence permit) - AHV insurance number (the number assigned by the Swiss social insurance system) - If your children are attending education or training: certificate of enrollment at a recognized educational or training institution - Declaration that you have not already submitted an application to another fund (to avoid double payments)
This documentation allows the cantonal fund to verify the applicant's identity, the paternity or maternity of the children, and their eligibility for benefits according to current regulations. Once the application with attached documents is sent, processing times are generally 2–4 weeks. During this period, the fund verifies the data, compares the information with the registers, and if everything is correct, authorizes the first payment. To see how these benefits affect your monthly [payslip simulation](nav:payslip), you can contact the compensation fund directly.
### Payment and Ongoing Benefit Management
Once the application is approved, family allowances are paid monthly to the bank account indicated by the applicant. The payment is automatic and continues as long as the conditions for eligibility persist — that is, as long as the children remain actually dependent and are still eligible according to the age and training status established by the canton. It is important to promptly inform the compensation fund of any relevant changes (change of residence, change in family situation, children finishing education or training, change of employer) so that payments remain correct and no improper arrears are generated.
For detailed information on the procedure, to download official forms, for the contact details of the compensation fund of the canton of Lucerne and the specific amounts valid for 2026, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to plan your family budget, or access directly the canton of Lucerne's portal in the section dedicated to Social Security and Family Allowances.

A Comparis analysis based on around 7.3 million cases reveals that repair costs for parking damage increased considerably between 2023 and 2025, well beyond the general inflation rate. In Switzerland, the situation is particularly acute for disassembly and structural repair work, while painting has recorded much smaller increases.
The most emblematic figure concerns the rear door: the average cost went from 92 francs in 2023 to 134 francs in 2025, an increase of almost 50%. The front doors have undergone similar increases. The side increased on average by 41%, while a front fender increased by 32%.
